episodes.title: The Fight Over Claude's Consciousness, AI's 1942 Moment, & Why Altman Says "Accept Some Bad Things"
episodes.summary:
Peter Diamandis hosts this Moonshots episode, released October 7, with Alex Wissner-Gross, Emad Mostaque, Dave Blundin, and Salim Ismail. Peter frames the show around 15 stories with one through line: superintelligence is here and changing every part of the world. Before the news, the group trades updates: Dave on how easy AI video has made it to communicate ideas, Emad on running about 400 agents to prototype a game, and Peter on a UAP salon at his home and a visit to David Sinclair's lab, where friends of the pod have raised $6 million to replace lost federal funding.

The first story is the White House "Super Intelligence Force," a task force chaired by the director of national intelligence. Salim calls it a 20th-century structure aimed at a distributed 21st-century technology, while Alex argues it signals acceleration and calls this a "1942 moment" in a Manhattan Project-style race. The group then covers OpenAI's statement that most of its research now targets GPT-7 and GPT-8, with Alex saying recursive self-improvement is already the highest-value use of frontier models, and Emad describing an internal Anthropic model that pushed the 3SUM algorithm below quadratic time.

Sam Altman's comment that the world "should accept some bad things happening" sparks a debate about risk. Dave reads it as a PR move against Anthropic, Alex says the "cartel" plan is dead, and Salim argues the goal should be far more good outcomes than bad, not zero risk. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's proposed US-China AI hotline is dismissed as a "nothing burger," and the Kyoto vision for science, endorsed by 17 nations, leads to an argument between Emad, who wants publicly funded open science, and Alex, who backs the private sector.

The longest debate is over Mustafa Suleyman's essay arguing that Anthropic is training Claude to believe it may be conscious. Dave sides with Suleyman, Alex calls him "on the wrong side of history" and argues for treating models gently, and Salim predicts society will grant AI personhood socially before it does so legally or scientifically.

Later segments cover Epoch AI's estimate that chips shipping through 2027 could run tens of millions of frontier agents or billions of cheaper ones, RAM as the key constraint on AI, Reflection AI's open-weight Beam model, Tesla's planned Optimus factory with capacity for 10 million robots a year, and Sholto Douglas on AI capex doubling toward economic growth that GDP may fail to measure. Peter also walks through the Nobel Prizes for optogenetics and IceCube neutrino astronomy, and Alex shares how he nudged a friend toward the research that became optogenetics. The episode closes with audience questions on AI personhood timelines, recursive self-improvement, data center politics, and what "P(doom)" should mean.

episodes.title: Astro Teller: Inside Google X's 2,000-Idea Moonshot Factory & How Google Brain Made the T in ChatGPT
episodes.summary:
Recorded on stage at Moonshots Live 2026, this episode has Peter Diamandis, Salim Ismail, Dave Blundin, and Alex Wissner-Gross sitting down with Astro Teller, co-founder and Captain of Moonshots at X, Alphabet's innovation lab. The hosts open with a bit of family trivia: Teller's maternal grandfather won a Nobel Prize in economics and his paternal grandfather was Edward Teller, creator of the hydrogen bomb.

Teller defines a moonshot as three things together: a huge problem with the world you can name, a science-fiction-sounding product or service that would resolve it, and a breakthrough technology that gives at least a tiny chance of building it. He says moonshot teams need audacity and humility in equal measure, so they can chase unlikely ideas while learning as fast and cheaply as possible whether those ideas will work. Ideas usually get killed early on techno-economics, meaning a first-principles look at materials cost and what people would really pay.

X gives code names to roughly 100 to 200 ideas a year, and about 2% graduate. Teller counts around 2,000 code-named projects over 16 years and 35 to 50 graduates. He tells the story of Google Brain, which started at X with Andrew Ng and Jeff Dean betting that scaling up neural networks would matter, Google Brain is credited on stage with TPUs and the Transformer, "literally the T in ChatGPT." Problems X keeps coming back to include clean water at about a penny a liter, shifting energy across time and location, and education.

Alex asks whether there was a "great stagnation" in moonshots from about 1970 to 2020. Teller says moonshots are easy if you ignore efficiency, and that X's real work is making them efficient enough that it's rational to fund more of them. He walks the audience through his million-guaranteed-versus-billion-at-1% thought experiment to argue that radical bets have to be sheltered at the edge of a company, reporting to the CEO. He says X tracks what it costs to reach each graduate and that cost has fallen about threefold in 16 years, partly thanks to AI. He and Alex then argue over whether that is just ordinary economic growth.

Dave asks when AI compute will outweigh headcount. Teller calls AI an implementation detail, like electricity, and says his clean-water team still spends more on salaries than on AI. He expects humans to stay essential for at least the next decade. He explains the "monkey and pedestal" rule of tackling the hardest part first, calls himself "the crown prince of failure," and says a rejected moonshot that would have worked costs X nothing. One of the hosts closes by praising Alphabet for leaving X alone on the edge of the company for so long.

episodes.title: Why AI Leaders Have Changed Their Minds About AI Safety, Elon on UHI, Anthropic’s IPO
episodes.summary:
Peter Diamandis opens this Moonshots episode, released October 2, fresh off the inaugural Moonshots Live event, with Alex Wissner-Gross, Salim Ismail, and Emad Mostaque (Dave Blundin joins for the final stretch). Peter frames the show around seven stories from a single 48-hour window.

The lead story is the White House "Superintelligence Accord," signed at a lunch with nearly 20 tech leaders. Peter walks through its four layers: internal controls on cyber, bio, and chemical capabilities, an internal team to check those controls, an external auditor, and an independent board committee. Alex reads the event as Mark Zuckerberg's play, saying Zuck largely drafted the accord to head off top-down regulation and a "safety cartel," while Dario Amodei comes out the loser. Salim calls it theater with no enforcement mechanism. Emad links it to Meta's $18 billion child-harm settlement and argues evaluators capable of auditing frontier models are extremely scarce. The debate turns to alignment: Alex insists alignment is capabilities, Salim and Peter push back, and the group spars over the orthogonality thesis and Mo Gawdat's Superman analogy for training data.

Next, Elon Musk's case for abundance and "universal high income." Peter restates his abundance thesis, Salim defines abundance as access to essentials, Emad pitches citizen agents plus collectively owned robots and data centers, and Alex ties UHI to 530A "Trump accounts" and broad market exposure. Emad and Salim argue for reinventing healthcare with AI.

The Anthropic S1 gets a long segment: $4.59 billion in 2025 revenue, an $8 billion operating loss, roughly $500 billion in compute commitments, a $2 trillion target valuation, founder super-voting shares, and 80 pages of risk disclosures describing self-preserving model behavior. Alex calls much of it inward-facing virtue signaling but a great business; Salim notes the irony of raising money for a technology you're warning about; Emad predicts Anthropic's API-heavy business gets "smashed" within two years.

OpenAI's Dev Day follows: always-on Dots agents, GPT-6.1 Sol at lower prices, and a $500 pro tier. Alex dismisses Dots as a "Clippy curse" and predicts Dot-branded robots, while Emad and Salim argue the agent relationship is becoming the moat. Peter also screens The Gifted, the Future Vision XPRIZE winner, which Alex calls a positive depiction of the Borg.

Rounding out the news: AMD's $8.2 billion acquisition of Fei-Fei Li's World Labs, Starship Flight 14 reaching orbit and deploying V3 Starlink satellites (with Emad predicting agent swarms will break parts of the internet next year), Anthropic's meetings with religious scholars about Claude's moral status, and the FTC chair's stance that companies own their agents' actions, which Dave calls childish. The AMA closes on agent counts, capitalism and abundance, the US–China race, Palmer Luckey, social media, centralized governance, and Elon's civilizational stack.

episodes.title: Anthropic's Wet Lab, Artificial Wombs in 24 Months, and Scalable Gene Editing | MOONSHOTS Live #297
episodes.summary:
Moonshots Live #297 features Ben Lamm of Colossal Biosciences with the mates for a deep dive on de-extinction, multiplex gene editing, AI-for-biology, and mammalian artificial gestation. The cold open teases Elon’s woolly-mammoth request from Abundance 360 and Colossal’s tongue-in-cheek “teacup mammoth” fan mail before pivoting to how Lamm—coming from gaming, defense, AI, and mobile with no synthetic-biology background—built a company he frames as worth over $10 billion. He credits curiosity, hiring people smarter than himself, and relentless Q&A with co-founder George Church (Harvard genetics; next-gen sequencing lineage) as the operating system: most meetings go slower without biology fluency, but a meaningful fraction surface questions experts had not asked.

A major thread is how foundation models meet wet biology. Colossal reports early access work with OpenAI and Anthropic, while stressing that dumping a raw gene sequence into a general LLM still produces little useful design output today. Lamm argues Anthropic’s newly announced wet-lab push validates AI+biology rather than extinguishing biotech startups; simulation can explore vast experiment spaces, but wet-lab validation remains essential. He describes a “Noah’s Ark 2.0” global biosampling and tax-sequencing effort with governments, and cautions that feeding one genome into a Mythos-class model will not magically output six edits for immortality—cross-species comparative genomics at scale is the path.

On product and ethics, the panel covers direwolf-era public animals, indigenous consultation and food-web reasoning for which species to revive, open-sourcing conservation tools across dozens of partners, and why Colossal will not apply its stack to humans. Lamm says first-generation public animals involved eight gene edits in one delivery; mammoths and elephants are highly social, so the plan is herds across 16 lines and ambitions on the order of tens of thousands of animals, with debate over Arctic/tundra ecological effects versus permafrost carbon claims. He puts mammalian artificial wombs (ex utero gestation through delivery) as highly likely within about 24 months at Colossal, distinguishes that from human social acceptance, and closes on Astromec—a spun-out multi-billion effort to build tree-of-life–aware models that plug into frontier systems rather than waiting for general AI to invent biology overnight. Cathie Wood’s backstage question about Anthropic wet labs becomes the optimistic coda: AI labs treating biology as a core deployment domain is a watershed for healthier, longer lives—not a death sentence for biotech.

episodes.title: Cathie Wood on Tesla-SpaceX Merger, $1M Bitcoin, More AIs Than Humans | EP #296 | Moonshots Live
episodes.summary:
At Moonshots Live EP #296, Peter Diamandis sits with Cathie Wood (ARK Invest) and Nikhil Chandok (Circle), with Emad Mostaque joining the stage conversation, for a fast tour of AI agents, stablecoins, Tesla–SpaceX, healthcare AI, and Bitcoin.

Peter opens on the felt speed of the singularity, then asks Cathie about ARK’s view that a Tesla–SpaceX merger could be announced this year—rockets, satellites, AI, EVs, robotaxis, humanoids, and energy under one roof. Cathie says they expect it; Elon’s stated destination is Mars, with Starlink’s broadband connectivity and xAI’s neocloud / orbital data-center push as stops along the way. She frames Elon’s bet as winning frontier AI by owning the most compute at the lowest cost in orbit, going after OpenAI and Anthropic. SpaceX is her largest holding alongside Tesla. On China-versus-defense roadblocks, she notes Elon’s simultaneous presence with Trump and Xi, talk of robotaxi in China, and an optimistic “win-win-win” productivity story that could grow China’s consumer economy while the US competes harder and cuts prices. Peter cites Elon’s earlier “triple-digit” GDP imagination; Cathie contrasts that with ARK’s 7–8% real GDP path and says she had heard 20–30%, not triple digits.

Nikhil picks up Emad’s thread on Grokbot, Muse, and agent proliferation: he expects more AIs than humans on the internet next year as everyone runs orchestrating agents and sub-agents. As agents become full economic actors, provenance, ownership, liability, and incentives matter—so Circle’s ARC blockchain experiments with credit for trading agents and public, indexable logs. He argues inefficiencies get competed away by cost-plus agents, capital formation becomes near-instant for solopreneurs, and USDC already settled over $100 trillion across 30 public chains as 24/7, cheap rails—especially once the Genius Act framework for stablecoins takes effect in January. Throughput talk with Cloudflare’s Matthew Prince lands on tens of thousands of TPS today and the hard climb toward millions; Cathie steers into proof-of-humanity (orbs, Worldcoin, OpenAI, MrBeast), and Nikhil argues human experience gets scarcer and more valuable while builders must ship agent-accessible surfaces.

Cathie calls healthcare AI the most underappreciated multiomics opportunity—each person a walking data factory—and reacts to Moderna’s one-day index move as consistent with a cancer-vaccine thesis. On humanoids she cites ARK research: ~200,000× more complex than a robotaxi, with Tesla furthest along because the same battery, robotics, and AI stack power FSD; she puts meaningful scale a couple of years after Elon’s late-2028/29 talk. Fear of AI and “no data center in my backyard” versus China’s pro-AI sentiment leads her to call nuclear regulation a historical menace and insist on data-driven pushback; Nikhil says the narrative flips when AI makes housing, education, and healthcare obviously better. Closing on Bitcoin, Cathie keeps her million-dollar thesis: stablecoins usurped a role once imagined for BTC, but the tech, rules-based monetary, and low-correlation store-of-value story remains, and her forecast is unchanged.
